medium.titulo: HubSpot’s Self-Updating CRM: What Changes When Your CRM Maintains Itself?
medium.resumo: The CRM used to depend on people keeping it updated.
medium.conteudo_html:
The CRM used to depend on people keeping it updated. HubSpot is betting that AI can take over that job — but that creates a bigger question about who checks what the CRM learns.

Every CRM conversation eventually comes back to the same problem. The data is only as good as what people put in — and people, reliably, put in less than they should. Calls go unlogged. Meeting notes are vague or missing. Records drift from reality as contacts change roles, companies shift, and deals move forward without anyone updating the stage.

HubSpot’s Fall 2026 Spotlight release takes direct aim at that problem. The redesigned Smart CRM is built around a simple premise: instead of waiting for employees to update customer records, HubSpot AI captures context from calls, emails, and meetings automatically and keeps the CRM current without requiring someone to remember.

That’s a meaningful shift. But it creates a question that’s worth thinking through carefully: if the CRM is maintaining itself, who is responsible for making sure it stays right?

The CRM Was Always Dependent on Humans

For most of the history of CRM software, the system was only as current as the last person who touched it.

Sales reps knew they should log calls. They often didn’t, because logging took time away from selling and the CRM wasn’t going to remind them. Admins spent hours cleaning up records that had drifted — duplicate contacts, outdated job titles, pipeline stages that hadn’t moved in months. Marketing built segments from data that was technically in the system but practically unreliable.

The manual maintenance burden was always the soft underbelly of CRM adoption. Hubspot CRM data quality Teams worked around it, tolerated it, or cleaned it periodically and watched it drift again. The CRM was only as accurate as the last update, and updates depended entirely on human initiative.

HubSpot Is Changing That Model

HubSpot’s Smart CRM changes the assumption. Calls, emails, and meetings are now captured and synchronized automatically. Customer context updates as interactions happen, rather than waiting for a rep to write up their notes after a call they half-remember.

Context Home — a new feature in the Fall 2026 release — gives organizations a score for how complete their contextual data is and surfaces gaps that could affect how well HubSpot’s AI agents perform. It’s a signal that HubSpot isn’t just automating data capture. It’s treating context quality as a measurable property of the CRM, one that directly affects what the AI can do with it.

The Breeze Assistant sits on top of all of this. Rather than answering questions from a generic AI context, it grounds its responses and actions in what’s actually in the CRM — the real conversation history, the actual account context, the current deal status. The self-updating CRM is, in part, what makes that grounding possible.

The Interesting Part Isn’t Automation. It’s Trust.

Here’s where it gets worth thinking carefully.

When a rep manually logged a call, they made a judgment call about what mattered. They decided which details to capture, which context was relevant, how to characterize the conversation. That judgment was imperfect — often too brief, sometimes omitted entirely — but it was human interpretation applied to a human interaction.

When AI captures and interprets the same call, different questions arise. What did the system decide was relevant? How was ambiguity handled? If a prospect said something that could be interpreted two ways, which interpretation made it into the record? If context was incomplete — the call cut short, the email thread missing earlier history — how did the system fill in the gaps?

A manually updated CRM had reliability problems that came from human inconsistency. A self-updating CRM has reliability problems that come from AI interpretation. The errors look different, propagate differently, and require different methods to catch.

The trust question isn’t whether HubSpot’s AI is capable. It’s whether your team has the visibility to know when the CRM’s understanding of a customer diverges from reality — and what the process is for correcting it when it does.

CRM Admins Aren’t Disappearing

The obvious reading of a self-updating CRM is that it reduces the work required to maintain it. That’s partially true. The hours spent chasing reps to log their activities, running deduplication scripts, and cleaning up fields that were never filled in consistently — some of that genuinely goes away.

But the nature of CRM management shifts rather than shrinks.

Less time on data entry doesn’t mean less responsibility for data quality. It means the focus moves upstream. Instead of correcting bad inputs after the fact, the work becomes defining what good context looks like, setting the rules that govern how interactions are captured and classified, and reviewing whether the automated updates reflect what’s actually happening in customer relationships.

Context Home gives admins visibility into completeness scores, which is useful. What it doesn’t replace is the judgment required to evaluate whether the context being captured is accurate, not just present. A CRM record can be complete and wrong at the same time.

What Happens When AI Builds on Bad Context

This is the part that matters most for businesses running HubSpot seriously.

A CRM record isn’t just a historical log anymore. Breeze AI agents use that context to generate recommendations, prioritize leads, trigger workflows, draft outreach, and take actions across the HubSpot platform. An incorrectly captured conversation detail doesn’t just sit in a record — it becomes an input for the next automated decision.

If AI mischaracterized a prospect’s objection in a call summary, the next AI-generated follow-up might address the wrong concern. If an account’s status was updated incorrectly based on an ambiguous email thread, an agent prioritizing renewals might act on that status. The error compounds because the system is designed to use context, not to verify it.

This isn’t an argument against the self-updating CRM. It’s an argument for treating what it captures with the same governance discipline that previously applied to what people entered.

The Definition of “Clean Data” Is Changing

Traditional CRM data quality had a relatively simple definition: is the record complete and up to date? Did the rep fill in the required fields? Is the contact information current?

For a CRM that feeds AI agents, the definition has to expand. The question isn’t just whether the fields are populated — it’s whether the context is accurate enough for an AI system to act on without producing unreliable outputs.

That’s a higher bar. And it requires a different kind of review. Completeness scores like Context Home are a start. But completeness is a proxy for quality, not the same thing. A CRM full of automatically captured but poorly interpreted interactions can score well on completeness while being genuinely unreliable as a foundation for AI-driven decisions.

What Businesses Should Check

Before trusting a self-updating CRM to power AI-driven workflows, a few things are worth reviewing — not as a checklist, but as honest questions.

Are important customer interactions being captured accurately, or just captured? Automatic logging is only valuable if what gets logged reflects what actually happened. Spot-checking AI-generated summaries against actual call recordings is worth doing periodically.

Can AI-generated updates be reviewed and corrected? If something is captured incorrectly, is there a clear process for identifying the error and fixing it before it propagates into downstream decisions?

Are permissions and data access configured for what’s actually being captured now? More automatic data capture means more data in the system. It’s worth reviewing who can see what, and whether the access model still fits.

Are the AI workflows built on top of this CRM designed for reliable context — or are they assuming perfect data they’re unlikely to get?

The Bigger Shift

The CRM used to be a place where customer history lived, as accurately as the people maintaining it could make it. The emerging model is different. HubSpot’s Smart CRM is designed to participate in maintaining its own understanding of the customer — continuously, automatically, in the background.

That’s genuinely useful. It also means the question of who is responsible for the CRM’s accuracy changes shape. The answer used to be: the people updating it. The new answer is more distributed — the AI doing the capturing, the admins setting the rules, the team reviewing the outputs, and the organization deciding how much to trust what the system concludes.

The future of CRM may not be about getting people to update the database. It may be about building a CRM you can trust to update itself — and having the oversight in place to know when it’s getting things right.

At Amroar Technologies, we help businesses build HubSpot environments that are ready for AI — from data architecture and governance to the oversight that makes automated CRM updates reliable rather than just fast.

medium.titulo: Here is why your design projects always take longer than you planned.
medium.resumo: You look at a design brief, the requirements are clear, you already have an idea of how you want to approach it.
medium.conteudo_html:
You look at a design brief, the requirements are clear, you already have an idea of how you want to approach it. So you think, “I should be able to finish this in three days.”

Then the work begins

- Research takes longer than expected,

- You discover a problem you didn’t account for,

- A user flow needs to change,

- Feedback introduces new iterations, that “small change” turns into several more.

Before you know it, the three-day project has become a week. This is where Hofstadter’s Law comes in, which state: It always takes longer than you expect, even when you take into account Hofstadter’s Law.

I think this is particularly relevant to UX because design is rarely a straight line. You don’t always know what you’ll discover during research. You can’t predict every round of feedback.

And sometimes, solving the actual problem requires going back to something you thought was already finished. So when planning your next project, don’t only estimate the time you’ll spend designing. Account for the time you’ll spend thinking, exploring, testing, revising and sometimes starting over.

A realistic timeline isn’t one where everything goes according to plan.

It’s one that leaves room for the plan to change.

medium.titulo: I Wasted Millions of Tokens Copy-Pasting Context. Then I Found These 6 Free Claude Connectors.
medium.resumo: For weeks I was doing something embarrassing.
medium.conteudo_html:
For weeks I was doing something embarrassing.

Pasting emails into a blank chat, losing the thread every single time, then retyping names and dates I had already typed the day before.

I went looking on Reddit to see if I was the only one doing this, and I wasn’t even close.

Half the threads about Claude were people venting about the exact same loop.

Paste something in, lose the formatting, lose the context, start over.

One person described pasting from Gmail and watching every line break disappear.

Another was manually copying budget numbers from a spreadsheet into chat, line by line, like it was 2009.

That’s when I actually looked into Claude connectors, and I felt a little silly for not doing it sooner.

What a Connector Actually Does ?

A connector is a permission link.

It lets Claude read what I approve inside an app I already use, and it only acts after I confirm the action myself.

That’s the whole idea.

Nothing gets sent or edited quietly in the background.

The Claude connectors directory lists six apps that cover almost everything I do in a normal week: Gmail, Calendar, Drive, Notion, Slack, and Canva. Setup is the same for all six.

Open the directory, choose the app, sign in, then toggle it on for the chat you’re using.

Claude inherits my own access to each app.

It can’t see anything I couldn’t already open myself, and writes stay on approval every time, so nothing gets sent without me reading it first.

1. Gmail

My inbox was the first place where copy-paste became ridiculous.

I would open an email, paste the thread into Claude, explain the customer and previous conversation, then ask for a reply.

Another email needed the same treatment.

With Gmail connected, I can ask:

Using Gmail, find unread customer emails from this week and group them by urgency. Draft replies for anything that needs an answer.

Claude can search and read email, draft replies and, where enabled, send or reply to messages.

Anthropic says approval is requested by default for those actions.

The useful part is the thread context.

I am no longer asking Claude to understand a pasted paragraph. I am asking it to look at the actual conversation.

Setup: Open Claude, add Gmail from the connectors area, authenticate, enable it for the chat, then name the sender, date range or email type.

2. Calendar

Calendar sounds small until your week gets packed.

I used to scan Monday through Friday, find empty spaces, then decide where deep work should go. It was work I kept repeating.

Now I can ask:

Using Google Calendar, find my busiest days next week and suggest two focus blocks that do not conflict with meetings.

Claude can view calendars and events, find availability, and create or update events when the connected setup allows it.

The trick is asking for a constraint, not a summary. “What is on my calendar?” gives me information.

“Find two uninterrupted focus blocks” gives me something usable.

Setup: Connect Google Calendar, enable it in the chat, mention the week, and state the rule you care about.

3. Drive

This one saved me from the folder maze.

I have had the same experience people describe on Reddit: the connector can look connected in settings, while the chat still does not use it until you enable it from the chat connector menu.

Once it is active, I can say:

Using Google Drive, find the latest budget sheet in the Finance folder and summarize the three biggest changes from last month.

Claude’s Google Drive connector can search and retrieve files, read documents and common file types, and work with metadata and permissions according to the connected account.

My best habit is naming the folder and file type. “Find my budget” is vague.

“Find the budget spreadsheet in Finance” gives Claude a smaller search space.

One warning: when multiple Google accounts are involved, check which account is authenticated.
Reddit users have reported account-selection confusion.

4. Notion

My meeting notes were always somewhere.

The annoying part was turning them into work.

I would open Notion, skim the notes, copy actions into Claude, then rewrite them as tasks.

With Notion connected:

Using Notion, search this week’s meeting notes for decisions, blockers and unfinished actions. Turn them into tasks with owners and due dates where they are already mentioned.

Notion is listed in Claude’s marketplace with search and update capabilities.

I like this because Claude sees the workspace where the notes already live instead of isolated pasted text.

Important distinction: I do not ask it to invent owners or deadlines.

If the note does not contain one, I would rather see “owner missing” than a confident guess.

That small rule makes the output more trustworthy.

5. Slack

Slack is where context disappears fastest.

A busy channel can contain jokes, decisions, status updates, links and side conversations before lunch.

I used to scroll until I felt caught up, usually becoming late to the work itself.

With Slack connected:

Using Slack, summarize what changed in the launch channel since yesterday. Separate decisions, blockers and useful links, and include the relevant threads.

Slack is a Anthropic verified connector that can fetch data, create canvases and send messages.

Claude also lists Slack among its interactive connectors.

For me, the value is filtering.

I do not need every message.

I need the messages that change what I should do next.

6. Canva

I did not expect Canva to matter this much for content work.

Before it, I would finish an article and then stare at a blank Canva file thinking, “Now I need a thumbnail.”

The Canva connector can search designs, inspect content, generate designs, autofill and export through Claude.

So I can start with:

Using Canva, create a simple editorial image for this article. Keep the headline readable, use my existing brand style, and make the design easy to edit.

This works better than asking for “a cool graphic.”

I give Claude the article, audience and visual constraint, then review the actual design.

A generated design is not automatically a good design.

The Setup That Finally Fixed My Broken Workflow

I stopped thinking of connectors as six separate AI tricks.

They are six doors into the places where my work already happens.

  • Gmail gives me the conversation.
  • The calendar gives me the schedule.
  • Drive gives me the source files.
  • Notion gives me working notes.
  • Slack gives me team context.
  • Canva gives me the visual.

Then comes the part Claude connectors do not solve by themselves: turning a finished idea into a complete article with research, links, images and a publishing path.

That is where I use Kitful

I do not treat it as another Claude connector.

I use it as the next workspace when the job changes from “help me think” to “help me finish this for the website.”

Kitful’s current workflow combines research, article creation, internal links, images and publishing in one website-specific workspace.

It can learn your voice from published content, a URL or a file, and it supports WordPress, Ghost, Shopify, Framer and webhooks.

The handoff is simple:

  1. Ask Claude to gather context from Gmail, Notion, Drive or Slack.
  2. Turn that context into a clean article brief.
  3. Move the brief into Kitful when the work needs research, images, internal links and publishing.
  4. Review before publishing.

That separation feels cleaner: Claude pulls together information already inside my work apps, while Kitful turns it into a website-ready piece.

One thing I Would Not Skip

Connectors are permissioned access, not a magic tunnel into everything.

Claude says connectors inherit your existing service permissions.

Google Workspace connectors keep approval in the loop for actions such as sending email or changing files by default.

So my rule is boring on purpose:

  • Read first.
  • Draft second.
  • Approve third.
If a connector is acting strangely, check the chat-level toggle before disconnecting everything.

That issue comes up repeatedly in Reddit discussions about Google Drive.

Keep the request narrow.

Tell Claude the app, folder, channel, calendar or date range.

Better context comes from less ambiguity, not a giant prompt.

Six prompts I would actually Use in My Workflow

Using Gmail, find unread customer emails from this week and draft replies for approval.
Using Google Calendar, find two uninterrupted focus blocks next week around my meetings.
Using Google Drive, find the latest finance spreadsheet and summarize the biggest changes.
Using Notion, find this week’s meeting decisions and turn confirmed actions into tasks.
Using Slack, summarize launch decisions and blockers since yesterday with thread references.
Using Canva, create an editable article graphic using my existing brand style.

FAQs

What Can a Claude Connector Reach?

A connector reaches only what I can already open in that app. It reads mail, events, files, pages, messages and designs when I ask. It acts only after I approve the draft.

How Do I Turn on Connectors?

I open the connectors menu from chat input or Customize in settings.

I pick an app in the Claude connectors directory, complete sign-in and toggle on for the chat.

Team workspaces need owner enablement before I sign in.

Why Keep Approval on for Sends?

Claude inherits my app access and can write where allowed.

I keep approval for send, edit and create and review before anything public.

Read-only keeps exposure low for research tasks.

What Still Needs Help After Drafting?

Drafting from notes works, but a post still needs research, images, links and publishing.

I use a blog workspace for those steps in one place. Claude hands off the draft and the workspace finishes it.

My Opinion

The first time connectors clicked, I realized how much of my day was spent reintroducing the same information.

That was the waste.

Now I open a chat, connect the source I need, and ask for the next useful action.

No giant paste.

No rebuilding the background story.

No jumping between six tabs just to explain what I am looking at.

And when that work becomes a blog post, I have a cleaner handoff instead of another blank page.

That is where Kitful fits naturally into the workflow.

Start with one connector.

Use it on one annoying task. Keep the approval step.

Once the copy-paste loop disappears in that one place, adding the next connector makes a lot more sense.

Thanks for reading.

medium.titulo: Why I Didn’t Pick the Most Popular Framework for My Game Site
medium.resumo: I built the same MVP with Next.js 14 and Vue 3 + Vite. Three days later, I realized the framework wasn’t the real decision at all.
medium.conteudo_html:
I built the same MVP with Next.js 14 and Vue 3 + Vite. Three days later, I realized the framework wasn’t the real decision at all.

Before I started building my game collection site, I spent a long time agonizing over the tech stack.

Next.js 14 is the popular choice right now. App Router + SSG looks perfect for a content site. Vue 3 + Vite is known for being lightweight — smaller first-load JS, faster builds. Both have good arguments. There are plenty of comparison articles online, but reading them only made me more indecisive. They all compared specs, but none of them told me how to choose given my constraints.

So I stopped reading and started building. Same MVP, two stacks, one after the other. Let the data decide.

What I found was something more important than the stack itself.

What I Actually Cared About

Most people start tech selection by comparing feature lists. But feature lists are infinite. What actually constrains you are just a few things. I wrote down three hard constraints:

One: SEO had to work. Most traffic for a game site comes from search engines. Game detail pages must be crawlable. This wasn’t “nice to have” — it was mandatory.

Two: First load had to be fast. LCP under 2.5s on mobile 4G. Users have only a few seconds of patience. Slow means gone.

Three: The game iframe couldn’t block the main thread. While browsing the list page, no game runtime code should load. I’ll come back to this point, because it turned out to be the real key.

These three constraints ended up driving my entire decision.

Day 1: Next.js Version — Static Export Taught Me a Lesson

I built the homepage, category pages, and game runtime page with Next.js 14 App Router, using output: 'export' for pure static export, deployed to Vercel.

Homepage and category pages generated HTML correctly. But /play/[id] all returned 404.

After digging in: App Router with output: 'export' doesn’t support dynamic routes by default unless you explicitly define generateStaticParams. This is heavily discussed in the community; developers have reported that “the latest Next.js App Router doesn’t support dynamic routes with static generation.”

Worse, even after defining generateStaticParams, all game IDs have to be pre-generated at build time. If the game count grows to hundreds, every new game triggers a full rebuild, and CI time grows exponentially.

I tried @falsefoundation/next-dynamic-exports, which supports dynamic routes by generating fallback pages, but it requires web server rewrite rules, adding deployment complexity.

Then I tried a different approach: turn the game runtime page from a dynamic route into a client-rendered static shell — the /play page reads the game ID via useSearchParams after loading. This bypasses the generateStaticParams limitation, but the game runtime page is no longer prerendered, so SEO suffers. My trade-off: the game runtime page has low SEO value anyway (users arrive from the detail page), so it’s acceptable.

Next.js version data: Homepage LCP 1.2s (mobile 4G throttling), first-load JS ~85KB (gzip), build time 12s.

（When publishing to Medium, embed the code snippets above via Gist to avoid formatting issues. Same for the rest of this article.）

Day 2: Vue 3 + Vite Version — Genuinely Lightweight

Vue’s dev experience was excellent. Vite cold start under 1 second, hot updates nearly imperceptible, build time only 6 seconds — half of Next.js. First-load JS ~50KB, nearly 40% less.

But SEO became a problem.

Vue + Vite defaults to SPA. The homepage and category pages only contain <div id="app"></div> in the HTML — crawlers see no content. The solution was to install vite-plugin-seo-prerender, which prerenders the SPA into static HTML files at build time.

Configuration is simple:

// vite.config.ts
import seoPrerender from 'vite-plugin-seo-prerender'

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [
    seoPrerender({
      routes: ['/', '/games/puzzle', '/games/sports']
    })
  ]
})

But the plugin has a limitation: it’s only suitable for generating static HTML for a small number of pages. If the game count grows to hundreds, every game detail page needs prerendering, and build time becomes uncontrollable.

Another option is Nuxt 3, Vue’s meta-framework with built-in SSG. But that introduces another framework, contradicting the “lightweight” goal.

Vue version data: Homepage LCP 1.5s (after prerendering), first-load JS ~50KB (gzip), build time 6s.

Day 3: A Counterintuitive Finding

After both versions were running, I did one thing: recorded the full timeline from homepage to clicking “Start Game” using Chrome DevTools Performance panel on both.

Something counterintuitive came up: the performance difference between the two versions was far smaller than I expected.

The Next.js version had 35KB more first-load JS, but on 4G that’s about 200ms of download time. The real time sink while browsing the list page wasn’t the framework’s JS size — it was the game iframe initialization.

In the default implementation, the iframe was initialized when the game detail page mounted. Even if the iframe src pointed to an empty placeholder page, creating the contentWindow and initializing the sandbox environment still consumed main thread time. On a Moto G Power, that single operation took about 400ms.

The correct approach is the facade pattern: render only a lightweight static placeholder (thumbnail + play button) before the iframe mounts, and inject the actual iframe only when the user clicks “Start.” This matches Lighthouse’s recommendation for deferring third-party resources.

There’s a Next.js static wiki case in the DEV community that uses the facade pattern to move a YouTube iframe from hydration-time mount to click-time load, bringing mobile TBT down from destructive levels to acceptable.

This means: the framework choice’s impact on first-load performance is far smaller than the iframe initialization strategy’s impact.

I wrote this down because it directly changed my selection criteria. Before, I was comparing “whose first-load JS is smaller.” Now I was comparing “who makes the facade pattern easier to implement.”

Final Choice: Hybrid Architecture

Based on the three-day comparison, I made these decisions:

Static content pages (homepage, category pages, detail pages) use Next.js SSG.SEO works out of the box, no extra plugins. Dynamic routes have limitations, but the game detail page ID count is manageable (only 6 games initially). If the game count grows to 200+, a Headless CMS with ISR can be introduced, but that requires a server and breaks the zero-backend constraint.

The game runtime page uses an independent client-rendered shell. The game runtime page has low SEO value and doesn’t need prerendering. Use next/dynamicwith ssr: false to lazy-load the game iframe component, facade pattern: initialize the iframe only after the user clicks “Start.”

Here’s the concrete implementation:

// components/GameLauncher.tsx
'use client'
import { useState } from 'react'
import dynamic from 'next/dynamic'

const GameIframe = dynamic(() => import('./GameIframe'), {
  ssr: false,
  loading: () => <div className="h-full bg-zinc-900 animate-pulse" />
})

export default function GameLauncher({ game }) {
  const [started, setStarted] = useState(false)

  if (!started) {
    return (
      <button
        onClick={() => setStarted(true)}
        className="relative w-full aspect-video rounded-lg overflow-hidden"
      >
        <img src={game.thumbnail} alt={game.title} className="w-full h-full object-cover" />
        <div className="absolute inset-0 flex items-center justify-center">
          <svg width="64" height="64" viewBox="0 0 64 64">
            <circle cx="32" cy="32" r="30" fill="rgba(0,0,0,0.6)" />
            <polygon points="26,20 26,44 46,32" fill="white" />
          </svg>
        </div>
      </button>
    )
  }

  return <GameIframe src={game.entry} gameId={game.id} />
}

ssr: false ensures the iframe component isn’t bundled into the HTML during server rendering, and only loads from the client after the user clicks. This matches Next.js’s official lazy-loading advice: for heavy components that don’t participate in SSR, use next/dynamic with ssr: false to reduce the initial bundle.

The Vue version wasn’t maintained. It builds faster and has a smaller bundle, but SEO needs extra plugins, and if the game count grows, the prerendering solution’s scalability is worse than Next.js’s SSG system.

Data Comparison

MetricNext.js 14Vue 3 + ViteFirst-load JS (gzip)~85KB~50KBHomepage LCP (4G)1.2s1.5s (after prerendering)Build time12s6sDynamic route supportNeeds generateStaticParamsBuilt-inSEOOut of the boxNeeds extra pluginsGame runtime lazy loadnext/dynamic native supportManual implementation

Test conditions: MacBook Pro M1 build, iPhone 12 + Chrome DevTools 4G throttling, 10 runs each, median.

Note a counterintuitive result: Vue’s LCP was actually slower than Next.js after prerendering. The reason is that vite-plugin-seo-prerender still includes the full Vue runtime in the generated HTML, while Next.js SSG outputs cleaner HTML with lower hydration cost. This shows that “smaller first-load JS” doesn’t equal “faster first load.”

（When publishing to Medium, turn this table into an image, since Medium doesn’t handle Markdown tables well.）

Trade-offs

Next.js build time is longer. 12s vs 6s. Every new game requires a rebuild. If the game count reaches 50, build time could exceed 30 seconds.

The Vue version was abandoned. It has better dev experience and a smaller bundle, but needs extra work on SEO and scalability. If your game site doesn’t need SEO — an internal tool or pure entertainment site — Vue + Vite is the better choice.

The hybrid architecture adds complexity. Static pages and the runtime page use different rendering strategies, requiring understanding of two sets of logic.

Unresolved

If the game count exceeds 100, generateStaticParams full pre-generation becomes a bottleneck, requiring ISR or a Headless CMS — but that’s no longer zero-backend.

I didn’t dig deep into Vue’s prerendering solution. vite-plugin-prerender-staticsupports multi-route generation and SEO meta tags, which might be enough if the game count is small.

Astro is another direction worth watching. A developer built a 50+ game site with Astro + vanilla JS, keeping the JS bundle under 100KB gzip and emphasizing “each game only loads the JavaScript it actually needs.” This approach is in the same spirit as the facade pattern. If you’re in the selection phase, it’s worth half a day to look into.

What This Means for You

If you’re making a similar tech decision, here’s my advice:

Define your hard constraints first, then look at frameworks. If your constraints are the same as mine (SEO + first load + iframe not blocking the main thread), the real decision point isn’t “Next.js or Vue” — it’s “how to implement the facade pattern.” The framework is just a container. Pick one whose downsides you can live with.

Don’t just look at first-load JS size. The Vue version was 35KB smaller, but its LCP after prerendering was actually slower. The relationship between size and performance is more complex than a spec sheet suggests.

Building both versions for three days is more useful than reading thirty comparison articles. The point of this article isn’t to tell you to pick Next.js. It’s to show you how to reach your own conclusion.

Full Code

Both MVP versions are organized, including Next.js and Vue comparison branches. The test data comes from a local environment. If you get different results on real hardware, I’d love to hear about it.

This article is based on my own project’s selection notes. AI was used only for grammar checking and structural suggestions; the technical judgments and test data come from actual runs.

medium.titulo: Migrating From Vue 2 to Vue 3: A 3-Year Journey
medium.resumo: A story about a failed rewrite, a three-year migration, and the lesson that came out of it.
medium.conteudo_html:
A story about a failed rewrite, a three-year migration, and the lesson that came out of it.

Three years ago, I decided to upgrade our frontend — a large, Vue 2 and Vuex-based IoT platform — to Vue 3. I didn’t know at the time that it would take three years, involve a failed rewrite, a full UI revamp, and a side project that turned into my first published npm package. Here’s how it actually went.

The problem

I could already see it getting worse, not better — an outdated stack meant losing access to newer package support and missing out on the AI tooling being built for modern ecosystems.

Our frontend couldn’t run past Node 14. Vue 2 and Vuex were becoming obsolete, and it was taking a real hit on productivity: the dev server had gotten painfully slow, changes took a long time to reflect while developing, and new plugins had essentially stopped coming out for the stack. It was time to rebuild.

Attempt #1: starting from scratch

My first instinct was to do it the “right” way — start a brand-new project from scratch, outside working hours, as a proof of concept, with a clean architecture from day one.

It failed quickly. Every time a new change landed in the live product, I had to replicate it in the new codebase and test everything twice. I couldn’t keep up the pace, so I abandoned the idea.

The pivot: migrating in place

Instead of starting fresh, I decided to migrate the existing project directly. The one requirement I had going in was to keep the git history intact, so the changes stayed traceable and in sync with everything that came before.

Roughly what that looked like:

  • Removed the main configuration files needed to run the project, without touching the existing modules yet
  • Removed package.json entirely — every package was obsolete and incompatible with Vue 3, since the jump from Vue 2 to Vue 3 changed too much under the hood for any of them to carry over
  • Installed Pinia as the new store, added Vue Router for Vue 3, and set up TypeScript support
  • Commented out every route, then brought them back one at a time, fixing whatever broke along the way

The component library grind

This part applies no matter which component library you’re using: whatever version supports Vue 3 usually isn’t backward-compatible with how you were using the old one, so you end up touching almost every file that references it.

There wasn’t a single clean diff to apply — most usages stayed the same, and only a handful of patterns had actually changed. So I kept a running to-do list of whatever I found different and worked through the fixes incrementally, file by file, over time, alongside the regular folder restructuring and the move to TypeScript.

Three years later

The numbers, for what they’re worth: our CI build on Jenkins dropped from about 5 minutes to 2. The local dev server used to take roughly 20 seconds to spin up — now it’s close to instant. We’re finally on a supported Node LTS release instead of being stuck on Node 14. The whole thing just feels smoother to work in, day to day.

It was, in every sense, a three-year ultra marathon. But we came out the other side with a fully current set of dependencies and a codebase that’s actually pleasant to build on again.

The problem I didn’t see coming

Once the migration was done, I ran into something I hadn’t planned for: the client couldn’t tell that anything had changed, because the UI still looked exactly the same as before.

All that work, and from the outside, nothing looked different.

So that became the next project — a full UI revamp, .done in close collaboration with design, business, and the development team — going stakeholder by stakeholder until everyone signed off. We made the interface more user-friendly and better looking.

A detour: building my own npm package

Partway through, I hit a wall — I couldn’t find a Vue 3-compatible version of an image upload package we depended on. So I built one myself and published it to npm as vue-crop-upload. It was a good excuse to learn something new, and it's out there now for anyone else who runs into the same gap.

The lesson

Starting from scratch looked like the “right” way to do this on paper. It wasn’t the right way for our circumstances — we couldn’t pause feature work or run two codebases side by side while rebuilding everything from zero.

The incremental, in-place migration was slower to look impressive and far less satisfying to plan out. It was also the one that actually worked. Sometimes the best solution isn’t the best solution for your circumstances — the one that fits your team, your timeline, and your constraints usually wins.

Thanks for reading — if you’ve gone through something similar, I’d love to hear how you approached it.

corrida_no_ar.resumo: Tigst Assefa vence e bate recorde em Berlim mesmo lesionada. O novo Adidas Adios Pro 5 apresenta problemas. Núbia de Oliveira é bicampeã das Dez Milhas Garoto e a Maratona de Salvador tem recorde de percurso e festa com É o Tchan!. Confira os resultados e bastidores.
corrida_no_ar.conteudo_html:
Segunda-feira | 28 de setembro de 2026

A etíope Tigst Assefa venceu mais uma vez a Maratona de Berlim, quebrando o recorde da prova com 2:11:04, mesmo após sofrer um rompimento parcial do tendão calcâneo durante o percurso. Ela estava a caminho de tentar o recorde mundial, mas a lesão a fez diminuir o ritmo. Imagens da chegada mostram a atleta mancando visivelmente, em uma demonstração de superação. Ao cruzar a linha, foi abraçada pela lenda do atletismo, Haile Gebrselassie. O pódio feminino foi completado por suas compatriotas Bedatu Hirpa (2:16:53) e Dera Dida (2:16:55).

No masculino, a vitória também foi da Etiópia, com Guye Adola, que marcou 2:02:50. O pódio masculino ainda teve Gemechu Dida Diriba, em segundo, com 2:03:19, e Gabriel Geay, da Tanzânia, em terceiro, com 2:03:59. Uma curiosidade da prova foi a ausência de atletas quenianos entre os 10 primeiros colocados, com um domínio etíope e a presença de um corredor japonês no top 10. Sisay Lemma, que era um dos favoritos, não largou.

Brasileiros em Berlim

A Maratona de Berlim contou com 50.073 concluintes, sendo 1.817 deles brasileiros. Entre os homens, o melhor brasileiro foi o incansável Paulo Paula, com o tempo de 2:12:07. Em seguida, vieram Antonio Pereira (2:19:53), Leonardo Santana (2:20:37), Vagner Noronha (2:20:44) e Miguel Morone (2:21:30).

No feminino, a melhor brasileira foi Amanda de Oliveira, com 2:36:45. Alice Yuri fez um impressionante recorde pessoal, terminando com 2:43:33. Completaram o top 5 Thalya Hillebrant (2:50:47), Rafaela de Souza (2:56:00) e Vanessa Brígido (2:56:33).

Problemas com o novo Adizero Adios Pro 5

O recém-lançado Adidas Adizero Adios Pro 5 tem sido alvo de polêmica. Vários corredores relataram problemas de durabilidade com o tênis, incluindo o descascamento do solado e a formação de bolhas, mesmo com poucos quilômetros de uso. As redes sociais foram inundadas com fotos e vídeos mostrando os defeitos. Apesar da repercussão e do alto preço do calçado, que custa R$ 2.200 no Brasil, a Adidas ainda não se pronunciou oficialmente sobre o assunto.

Dez Milhas Garoto agita o Espírito Santo

Na tradicional prova Dez Milhas Garoto, que liga Vitória a Vila Velha, Núbia de Oliveira sagrou-se bicampeã com um sprint final emocionante. Ela completou o percurso em 59min39s. A segunda e terceira colocadas foram as etíopes Kisha Fesaha (59min41s) e Arisley Ketema (59min44s).

No masculino, a vitória ficou com o queniano Nicholas Kosgei, que marcou 48min14s. O melhor brasileiro foi Giovani dos Santos, que chegou em segundo lugar com 48min31s. O pódio ainda teve Vestus Cheboi em terceiro (48min58s).

Maratona de Salvador: festa e recordes

A Maratona de Salvador foi um grande evento, com 7.092 concluintes nas quatro distâncias oferecidas. A prova de 42 km contou com 1.046 corredores. No masculino, Justino Pedro venceu e estabeleceu um novo recorde do percurso com 2:21:01. Divaldo Araújo Sena (2:25:14) e Iago Silva de Oliveira (2:26:51) completaram o pódio.

No feminino, a vitória foi de Vanecléa Moura dos Santos, com 2:45:17. A veterana Marily dos Santos foi a segunda colocada (3:07:54), seguida por Marina Gomes Marçal Gomes (3:19:25). A prova foi marcada por muita animação, bandas ao longo do percurso e uma grande festa na chegada com show do grupo É o Tchan!. Eu, Sérgio Rocha, participei da prova, mas não foi meu dia. Senti que o corpo não estava respondendo bem e, para evitar sofrimento, abandonei no km 18,5. A organização, no entanto, está de parabéns, com hidratação a cada 2 km e um ótimo clima.

Nos 21 km, a vitória masculina foi de João Marcos Santos Oliveira (1:07:12) e a feminina de Geane Barreto dos Santos (1:18:53).
